Dynamic diagram (deployment view): AWS document metadata sync and Azure on-demand retrieval.
Requirement: Cosmos DB in Azure decouples document discovery from AWS availability. If cross-cloud connectivity fails, metadata-based requests such as finding documents can still be served. The described live S3 retrieval path still depends on access to S3.

AWS Cloud contains a Document publishing service [Software system] as a truthful generic plain box, Amazon S3 as the document store, and Amazon SQS queues (x3: documents, templates, bundles). The producer's actual product/name is unknown; do not invent one. Azure Cloud contains Cosmos DB (NoSQL document metadata store), Azure Blob Storage (temporary document storage with a retention policy; no duration specified), and an Outbound workflows software system boundary. That boundary contains SQS listener workflows (x3), a Processing workflow and a Retrieving workflow, all Azure Logic Apps. The three listeners correspond to SQS-Document-Cosmos, SQS-Template-Cosmos and SQS-Bundle-Cosmos, one per record type/queue.

Network resolution for this synthetic fixture: use public HTTPS service endpoints between Azure and S3/SQS, not an assumed private connection or VPN. S3 requests use AWS Signature authentication. The exact producer identity, cloud region and retention duration are unspecified.

Flow A, write/metadata sync: when a document is published or a template version approved, the publishing service saves the document in S3 and publishes a metadata event asynchronously to the appropriate SQS queue. There is one queue per record type, not one combined queue. Azure's corresponding SQS listener polls SQS for messages using the SQS API over HTTPS; arrows point from listener to queue because the listener initiates polling, with returned events in the label. Each listener inserts or updates metadata in Cosmos DB by the record's identity. Preserve the three queue/listener types and the distinction between document content in S3 and metadata in Cosmos DB. Show A1 producer->S3 Save document [HTTPS], A2 producer->SQS Publish metadata event [async, SQS], A3 listener->SQS Poll [SQS API/HTTPS], returns events, and A4 listener->Cosmos DB Upsert metadata by record ID.

Flow B, read/retrieval: Processing workflow queries Cosmos DB for metadata and gets the S3 reference. It passes that reference to Retrieving workflow. Retrieving workflow gets the document from S3 over HTTPS using AWS Signature, saves it once to temporary Azure Blob Storage under its retention policy, and returns the blob reference to Processing workflow. Show B1 Processing->Cosmos DB as a dashed auxiliary query returning the S3 reference; B2 Processing->Retrieving passing the S3 reference and returning the blob reference on the same caller-to-callee relationship; B3 Retrieving->S3 Get document [HTTPS, AWS Signature]; B4 Retrieving->Blob Storage Save document temporarily. Do not duplicate the save-to-blob step or invent a direct Blob Storage->Processing callback.

Flow A and B are independently numbered/color-coded and explained in the legend; async is a label qualifier, not a new line style. Put the decoupling purpose in a concise requirement/comment. Business-specific publication/withdrawal/replacement status rules, database/container/key schemas, sample records and the retry/alarm table are intentionally outside this architectural diagram's scope and absent from this resolved L0. No producer identity or private network access is owner-confirmed by these test choices.

The diagram is titled “Dynamic diagram (deployment view): AWS document metadata sync and Azure on-demand retrieval.” It describes two independently numbered flows: A, write and metadata synchronization; and B, read and retrieval. The stated requirement is that Cosmos DB keeps metadata-based discovery available when cross-cloud connectivity fails. Live document retrieval still requires access to S3.

There are two deployment nodes, AWS Cloud and Azure Cloud. The cloud region is unspecified for each. AWS Cloud contains a Document publishing service, three individual Amazon SQS queues, and Amazon S3. The Document publishing service is a software system that publishes document content and metadata events. Its producer product/name is unspecified. A note identifies document publication or template-version approval as the occasion for publication.

The three AWS queues are “Amazon SQS — documents queue,” “Amazon SQS — templates queue,” and “Amazon SQS — bundles queue.” Each is a container using Amazon SQS and holds metadata events. Amazon S3 is a container using Amazon S3 and is the document content store.

Azure Cloud contains a software system boundary named “Outbound workflows.” Inside that boundary are five containers using Azure Logic Apps: three listener workflows named SQS-Document-Cosmos, SQS-Template-Cosmos, and SQS-Bundle-Cosmos; a Processing workflow; and a Retrieving workflow. Also inside Azure Cloud, but outside the Outbound workflows boundary, are Cosmos DB and Azure Blob Storage. Cosmos DB is a container using Azure Cosmos DB / NoSQL and is the document metadata store. Azure Blob Storage is a container using Azure Blob Storage and provides temporary document storage. A retention policy applies to the temporary storage, with duration unspecified.

Flow A is the write/metadata-sync flow, described as publishing content and metadata events, polling, and upserting. Its calls are:

1. A1: The Document publishing service calls Amazon S3 to “Save document [HTTPS].” This stays within AWS Cloud.
2. A2a: The Document publishing service publishes a metadata event to the documents SQS queue, labeled “[async, SQS] — documents.”
3. A2b: The Document publishing service publishes a metadata event to the templates SQS queue, labeled “[async, SQS] — templates.”
4. A2c: The Document publishing service publishes a metadata event to the bundles SQS queue, labeled “[async, SQS] — bundles.”
5. A3a: The SQS-Document-Cosmos listener initiates a poll of the AWS documents queue, labeled “Poll [SQS API / public HTTPS].” The response returns metadata events.
6. A3b: The SQS-Template-Cosmos listener initiates the same kind of poll of the AWS templates queue, using SQS API / public HTTPS and returning metadata events.
7. A3c: The SQS-Bundle-Cosmos listener initiates the same kind of poll of the AWS bundles queue, using SQS API / public HTTPS and returning metadata events.
8. A4a, A4b, and A4c: Respectively, SQS-Document-Cosmos, SQS-Template-Cosmos, and SQS-Bundle-Cosmos call Cosmos DB to “Upsert metadata by record ID [Cosmos DB].”

The three poll calls cross the Outbound workflows boundary and the Azure/AWS cloud boundaries, with each Azure listener as caller and its AWS queue as callee. The three upsert calls leave the Outbound workflows boundary but remain within Azure Cloud. The diagram explicitly shows three separate queues and their three corresponding listeners. No polling interval is specified. “Async” qualifies metadata publication; it does not change the line style.

Flow B is the read/retrieval flow, described as querying metadata, retrieving S3 content, saving once, and returning a blob reference. Its calls are:

1. B1: The Processing workflow queries Cosmos DB for metadata, labeled “Query metadata [Cosmos DB].” The response returns an S3 reference. This is an auxiliary query, drawn as a dashed line, from the Processing workflow inside Outbound workflows to Cosmos DB outside that boundary but within Azure Cloud.
2. B2: The Processing workflow calls the Retrieving workflow, labeled “Pass S3 reference [workflow call].” The response returns a blob reference. Both workflows are inside Outbound workflows.
3. B3: The Retrieving workflow calls Amazon S3 to “Get document [public HTTPS, AWS Signature].” The response returns document content. This crosses the Outbound workflows boundary and the Azure/AWS cloud boundaries, with the Azure Retrieving workflow initiating the call to S3.
4. B4: The Retrieving workflow calls Azure Blob Storage to “Save document temporarily [Azure Blob Storage].” This leaves Outbound workflows but stays within Azure Cloud. The temporary storage is subject to the retention policy whose duration is unspecified.

A connectivity note states that cross-cloud connectivity uses public HTTPS service endpoints and that S3 requests use AWS Signature. No more specific authentication mechanism is given for the other calls. The diagram provides no explicit initiating actor or trigger for the Processing workflow, and no detailed error code, retry rule, or allow/deny condition. Its explicit failure qualification is that metadata discovery remains available through Cosmos DB when cross-cloud connectivity fails, whereas live retrieval still depends on access to S3.

The legend says that a filled arrow means caller to callee. Normal responses are folded into the request labels rather than shown as separate response arrows. Dashed means the auxiliary query B1; solid means a main call. Cosmos DB stores metadata, while S3 and temporary Blob Storage hold document content. The A and B flow numbering is independent.

The Azure boundary contains a nested software-system boundary named “Outbound workflows — 5 workflows,” plus Cosmos DB and Azure Blob Storage outside that nested workflow boundary but inside Azure. The five workflows within the nested boundary are three SQS listener workflows, a Processing workflow, and a Retrieving workflow. All five are containers using Azure Logic Apps.

The metadata listeners are named “SQS-Document-Cosmos,” “SQS-Template-Cosmos,” and “SQS-Bundle-Cosmos.” Each is labeled a Listener workflow. There are three separate queues and three corresponding listeners, and the polling interval is unspecified. Cosmos DB is a container using Azure Cosmos DB / NoSQL and is the document metadata store. Azure Blob Storage is a container using Azure Blob Storage and provides temporary document storage. A temporary storage retention policy applies, but its duration is unspecified.

The A flow is the write / metadata sync flow, shown in blue. It publishes content and metadata events, polls, and upserts:

1. A1: The Document publishing service calls Amazon S3 to “Save document [HTTPS].” This call stays within AWS.
2. A2a: The Document publishing service publishes a metadata event to the documents queue, labeled “Publish metadata event [async, SQS] — documents.”
3. A2b: The Document publishing service publishes a metadata event to the templates queue, labeled “Publish metadata event [async, SQS] — templates.”
4. A2c: The Document publishing service publishes a metadata event to the bundles queue, labeled “Publish metadata event [async, SQS] — bundles.” These three publications stay within AWS and are asynchronous calls.
5. A3a: SQS-Document-Cosmos initiates a poll of the documents queue using “SQS API / public HTTPS.” The queue returns metadata events.
6. A3b: SQS-Template-Cosmos initiates a poll of the templates queue using “SQS API / public HTTPS.” The queue returns metadata events.
7. A3c: SQS-Bundle-Cosmos initiates a poll of the bundles queue using “SQS API / public HTTPS.” The queue returns metadata events. These polling calls cross from the Azure workflow boundary and Azure deployment into AWS; the arrows point toward the queues, expressing the listeners as callers.
8. A4a: SQS-Document-Cosmos calls Cosmos DB to “Upsert metadata by record ID [Cosmos DB].”
9. A4b: SQS-Template-Cosmos calls Cosmos DB to “Upsert metadata by record ID [Cosmos DB].”
10. A4c: SQS-Bundle-Cosmos calls Cosmos DB to “Upsert metadata by record ID [Cosmos DB].” Each upsert leaves the nested workflow boundary but stays within Azure.

The B flow is the read / retrieval flow, shown in orange. It queries metadata, retrieves S3 content, saves it once, and returns a blob reference. The Processing workflow’s initiating actor or trigger is not explicitly provided.

1. B1: The Processing workflow initiates “Query metadata [Cosmos DB]” against Cosmos DB and receives an S3 reference. This is an auxiliary query, shown with a dashed arrow from Processing workflow to Cosmos DB. It leaves the workflow system boundary while remaining inside Azure.
2. B2: The Processing workflow calls the Retrieving workflow to “Pass S3 reference [workflow call].” This call returns a blob reference. Both caller and callee are inside the five-workflow boundary.
3. B3: The Retrieving workflow calls Amazon S3 to “Get document [public HTTPS, AWS Signature].” S3 returns document content. This call crosses from the nested Azure workflow boundary, out of Azure, and into AWS.
4. B4: The Retrieving workflow calls Azure Blob Storage to “Save document temporarily [Azure Blob Storage] — save once.” This call crosses out of the nested workflow boundary while remaining inside Azure. Blob Storage holds the retrieved document content temporarily; the B2 workflow-call response supplies the blob reference to the Processing workflow.

Cross-cloud connectivity uses public HTTPS service endpoints. S3 requests use AWS Signature. Other authentication mechanisms are not specified. No detailed error code, retry rule, or allow/deny condition is provided. In a cross-cloud connectivity failure, metadata discovery remains available through Cosmos DB, while live retrieval still depends on access to S3.

The legend specifies that filled arrows mean caller to callee, with normal responses folded into the request labels rather than drawn as separate response arrows. Solid lines indicate main calls, including asynchronous publication; the dashed B1 line indicates an auxiliary query. The A and B numberings are independent. facts.claim: Retrieving calls S3 to obtain document content.
facts.evidence: The Retrieving workflow calls Amazon S3 to “Get document [public HTTPS, AWS Signature].” S3 returns document content.

facts.claim: Retrieving saves the retrieved document to Blob Storage.
facts.evidence: The Retrieving workflow calls Azure Blob Storage to “Save document temporarily [Azure Blob Storage] — save once.”

facts.claim: The retrieval flow saves document content to Blob Storage once.
facts.evidence: Save document temporarily [Azure Blob Storage] — save once.

facts.claim: Publisher-to-S3 document saving uses HTTPS.
facts.evidence: Save document [HTTPS]

facts.claim: Metadata publication uses SQS.
facts.evidence: [async, SQS]

facts.claim: Queue polling uses the SQS API over HTTPS.
facts.evidence: initiates a poll of the documents queue using “SQS API / public HTTPS.”

facts.claim: Azure-to-S3/SQS cross-cloud connectivity uses public HTTPS service endpoints.
facts.evidence: Cross-cloud connectivity uses public HTTPS service endpoints.

facts.claim: S3 requests use AWS Signature authentication.
facts.evidence: S3 requests use AWS Signature.

facts.claim: A retention policy applies to temporary Blob Storage.
facts.evidence: A temporary storage retention policy applies

facts.claim: The temporary storage retention duration is unspecified.
facts.evidence: but its duration is unspecified

facts.claim: The producer product/name is unspecified.
facts.evidence: Its producer product/name is unspecified.

facts.claim: Cloud regions are unspecified.
facts.evidence: “AWS Cloud — region unspecified” and “Azure Cloud — region unspecified.”

facts.claim: Cosmos DB keeps metadata-based discovery available if cross-cloud connectivity fails.
facts.evidence: Its stated requirement is that Cosmos DB keeps metadata-based discovery available when cross-cloud connectivity fails

facts.claim: Live retrieval requires access to S3.
facts.evidence: live document retrieval still requires access to S3.
